Longleaf pine
Pinus palustris
longleaf pine; longleaf yellow pine

An evergreen pine of the southeastern Coastal Plain, often with a tall clear trunk and open crown. Its exceptionally long needles occur three per fascicle; the large, prickly cones mature after pollination in a separate season.
Southeastern United States, from the coastal plain of Virginia south to Florida and west toward eastern Texas; chiefly sandy, fire-influenced pine habitats.

Bell heather
Erica cinerea
bell heather; Scotch heather
A low evergreen heath shrub with many fine branches and tiny narrow leaves in whorls of three. Its pink to purple urn-shaped flowers are borne in leafy clusters; each flower forms a small capsule.
Atlantic western Europe, especially dry acidic heaths and open moorland; locally on rocky ground.

Rannoch-rush
Scheuchzeria palustris
rannoch-rush; pod grass

A small rhizomatous bog perennial with erect, narrow, sheathing leaves. Its inconspicuous green flowers have six tepals; the fruit separates into three spreading follicles, a useful distinction from sedges.
Circumboreal in the Northern Hemisphere, in nutrient-poor peat bogs, fens and wet Sphagnum communities.

Hardy banana
Musa basjoo
hardy banana; Japanese fiber banana

A large rhizomatous herb whose apparent trunk is a pseudostem formed by overlapping leaf sheaths. The broad blades tear readily in wind; a hanging inflorescence bears flowers under purple bracts, followed by seedy, generally inedible berries.
Native to southern Sichuan, China; widely cultivated as an ornamental, including in Japan.

Columbia lily
Lilium columbianum
Columbia lily; tiger lily of the West

A bulbous western North American lily with an erect stem and narrow leaves often arranged in whorls. Its orange, dark-spotted flowers nod and have strongly recurved tepals; an erect capsule follows flowering.
Western North America, from British Columbia through the Pacific Northwest to California and inland mountain regions; open woods and meadows.

Nodding lily
Lilium cernuum
nodding lily
A slender bulbous lily with scattered narrow leaves and one or several nodding flowers. The pink to purple tepals are dark-spotted and roll back markedly; the fruit is an upright capsule.
Northeastern China, Korea and the Russian Far East, in grassy openings and woodland margins.

Many-flowered fawn lily
Erythronium pluriflorum
many-flowered fawn lily

A small spring geophyte of the central Sierra Nevada, arising from a deep bulb. Each flowering shoot usually carries two smooth green basal leaves and may bear several nodding golden flowers with recurved tepals.
High-elevation central Sierra Nevada, California, in moist meadows and open subalpine sites after snowmelt.

Lemon fawn lily
Erythronium citrinum
lemon fawn lily; citrine erythronium

A bulbous spring perennial with two mottled basal leaves and one to a few pale cream flowers, often yellow at the base. The tepals reflex at maturity; populations may intergrade with related western Erythronium, so identification can require locality and floral details.
Klamath-Siskiyou region of northern California and southwestern Oregon, often on serpentine or rocky soils.

Blue vanda
Vanda coerulea
blue vanda

An epiphytic orchid with a short monopodial stem, leathery strap leaves and aerial roots. Large flat blue-violet flowers bear tessellated darker veins and a notably small lip; spikes may carry many flowers.
From northeastern India through Myanmar and northern Thailand to southern Yunnan and Indo-China; often on exposed trees at about 900–1500 m.
Epiphytic orchid with short upright stem and aerial roots

Musk orchid
Herminium monorchis
musk orchid; one-bulb orchid

A small, glabrous terrestrial orchid with two or three bluish-green basal leaves and a slender, often one-sided spike of tiny yellow-green flowers. Each flower has a three-lobed lip, a loose hood and no spur; underground tubers connect by slender stolons.
Temperate Eurasia to the Himalaya, in short grassland and calcareous turf; habitat varies across its broad range.

Dark-red helleborine
Epipactis atrorubens
dark-red helleborine; red helleborine

A rhizomatous terrestrial orchid, usually 25–80 cm tall, with stem leaves often in two ranks and a many-flowered, commonly one-sided raceme. The brown-red to purple flowers are short-haired and often vanilla-scented; fruits are capsules.
Europe to western and central Asia, especially open pine woods and dry calcareous grassland from lowlands to subalpine elevations.

Neuwiedia griffithii
Griffith’s neuwiedia

A robust terrestrial apostasioid orchid with a stout rhizome and several large plicate leaves. Its pale flowers retain three free, functional stamens rather than the single fused column typical of most orchids; this family-level feature is diagnostic.
Southeast Asian Malesia, reported from the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Vietnam; shaded humid forest.

Poet’s daffodil
Narcissus poeticus
poet’s daffodil; pheasant’s-eye narcissus

A bulbous perennial with several narrow basal leaves and usually one flower per scape. Six white tepals surround a very short yellow corona with a conspicuous red crenulate rim; all parts, especially bulbs, contain toxic alkaloids.
Central and southeastern Europe, especially damp meadows and mountain grassland; widely planted and locally naturalised elsewhere.

Dracaena pethera
Sansevieria kirkii; Kirkii’s sansevieria

A stemless rhizomatous succulent now accepted as Dracaena pethera; Sansevieria kirkii is a synonym retained here to match the tree terminal. One to three rigid leathery leaves form a basal rosette, with conspicuously wavy, sometimes reddish margins; pale tubular flowers give way to orange-red berries.
Eastern and southeastern tropical Africa, in seasonally dry woodland and scrub; cultivated elsewhere.

Sotol
Dasylirion acrotrichum
sotol; Mexican grass tree

A slow-growing, usually solitary plant with a short woody stem and a dense spherical rosette of long narrow leaves. Margins bear small hooked teeth; mature plants send up a tall, narrow panicle of clustered pale flowers and later dry capsules.
Central Mexico, particularly upland semiarid scrub and rocky slopes; widely cultivated in dry gardens.

Lilyturf
Liriope muscari
lilyturf; monkey grass
An evergreen rhizomatous perennial forming dense clumps of arching, grasslike leaves. Upright spikes carry many small violet flowers with six tepals; rounded fruits mature dark purple to black.
Native to China and Taiwan; commonly cultivated as a groundcover in shaded gardens.

Alpine puya
Puya alpestris
alpine puya; sapphire tower

A large terrestrial bromeliad forming a basal rosette of stiff, spiny, grey-green leaves. Its tall branched inflorescence bears distinctive turquoise to blue-green flowers; the species is closely related to other Chilean Puyas, so flower colour alone should not be used for identification.
Central Chile, on dry rocky slopes and scrub at foothill to montane elevations.

Cabbage royal palm
Roystonea oleracea
cabbage royal palm; Caribbean royal palm

A towering solitary palm with a smooth grey trunk ringed by leaf scars and a conspicuous green crownshaft. Large pinnate fronds form the crown; cream inflorescences emerge below the crownshaft, followed by purplish-black single-seeded fruits.
Lesser Antilles south through Trinidad to northern Venezuela and northeastern Colombia; planted widely in the tropics.

Kentia palm
Howea forsteriana
kentia palm; thatch palm

A solitary, slow-growing palm with a slender ring-scarred trunk and a crown of arching pinnate fronds. Branched inflorescences emerge below the leaves; the ovoid fruits ripen from green to reddish brown.
Endemic to Lord Howe Island, where it grows in lowland and montane forest; extensively cultivated as an indoor palm.

Japanese royal fern
Osmunda japonica
Japanese royal fern; Asian royal fern

A robust terrestrial fern with an erect or short-creeping rhizome and large twice-pinnate fronds. Sterile fronds have broad toothed pinnules; fertile fronds bear narrow contracted pinnae densely covered with sporangia and shed them after spore release.
Eastern and southeastern Asia, in forests, wet stream margins, open slopes and grasslands from lowlands to mountains.
